# What item text tells us {#item-text}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain why predicting item difficulty from text is useful, and what it
  can and cannot replace;
* describe items by **text features** with `item_features()`, and connect
  them to the item covariates of the **linear logistic test model** (LLTM);
* predict difficulty with an explanatory model, a lasso and a random forest
  using `predict_difficulty()`, and compare them by **cross-validation**;
* fit the one-step LLTM to responses in mirt;
* recognize **leakage**, choose the right unit to hold out, and know the
  limit set by the error in estimated difficulties.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Feature](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#feature),
[LLTM](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#lltm),
[overfitting and cross-validation](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cross-validation),
[embedding](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#embedding),
[data leakage](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/ai-translation.html#data-leakage).

## The ideas

Every new item needs a difficulty before it can be used for scoring, and
the usual way to get one is a **field test**: The item is given to hundreds
of test takers and calibrated (Chapter \@ref(estimation)). Field testing is
slow and expensive, and it exposes items before they count. Item writers
also know that some features make items harder: More reading, an extra
step, a negation, decimals instead of whole numbers. If difficulty could be
**predicted from the text**, a program could target field-test forms, use
smaller field-test samples, steer item writing towards the difficulties the
bank lacks, and judge items written by a generator (Chapter \@ref(llms)).

Psychometrics and machine learning both have a way of doing this.

* **Explanatory IRT.** The linear logistic test model [@fischer1973]
  replaces each item's difficulty with a weighted sum of its features:
  $$b_i = \eta_0 + \sum_k \eta_k q_{ik},$$
  where $q_{ik}$ is the value of feature $k$ for item $i$ (the item's
  covariates) and $\eta_k$ is how much the feature adds to difficulty, in
  logits. The weights are read as evidence about *what makes items hard*,
  which is a claim about the construct [@deboeck2004]. The model can be
  fitted to the responses in one step, or in two steps by regressing
  estimated difficulties on the features.
* **Prediction.** Machine learning treats difficulty as a label to predict
  from as many features as are useful: Counts and readability measures,
  word frequencies, or **embeddings** of the text from a language model.
  Models such as the lasso or a random forest are judged by how well they
  predict items they were not trained on [@alkhuzaey2024; @benedetto2023].

The two are less different than they look. The two-step LLTM *is* a linear
regression, and the lasso is the same regression with its weights shrunk.
What differs is the goal: Explaining difficulty, or predicting it as
accurately as possible. Three cautions apply to both.

* **Leakage.** A feature computed from the same responses as the
  difficulty, such as the proportion correct in the field test, predicts
  difficulty almost perfectly and is useless, because it is not available
  until the item has been field-tested.
* **What is held out.** Items written from the same template (an [item
  model](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-model)) share most of their difficulty. A model
  that has seen other items from an item's template predicts it well; a
  model asked about a new kind of item usually does much worse. Cross-validation
  must hold out the unit you will predict for.
* **The noise floor.** Estimated difficulties have standard errors, and
  features never capture everything that makes an item hard. No model can
  predict $b$ more closely than its estimation error, and an LLTM rarely
  fits as well as giving every item its own difficulty. Real benchmarks
  show modest gains over simple baselines [@yaneva2024].

## Example 1: Features and an explanatory model

A science program has 70 multiple-choice items of the form *"Which of these
is a mammal?"*, on seven topics. Half the items are negated (*"Which of these
is NOT a mammal?"*), half start with a context sentence that adds reading
but no content, and in some the key happens to be the longest option, a
cue that test-wise students use. We simulate the items and the responses of
1,000 students, and calibrate the Rasch model.

```{r data-item-text-1}
# Simulated science classification items, with responses of 1,000 students.
set.seed(1414)
groups <- list(   # members, non-members and base difficulty of each topic
  mammal = list(yes = c("whale", "bat", "dolphin", "rabbit", "horse", "squirrel"),
                no = c("shark", "penguin", "frog", "crocodile", "salmon", "eagle"), b = -0.8),
  reptile = list(yes = c("lizard", "turtle", "snake", "crocodile", "gecko", "tortoise"),
                 no = c("frog", "salamander", "newt", "toad", "eel", "seal"), b = 0.2),
  insect = list(yes = c("ant", "beetle", "butterfly", "grasshopper", "bee", "dragonfly"),
                no = c("spider", "scorpion", "centipede", "tick", "crab", "snail"), b = 0),
  metal = list(yes = c("copper", "iron", "aluminium", "zinc", "silver", "tin"),
               no = c("glass", "wood", "plastic", "rubber", "sulfur", "carbon"), b = -0.3),
  conductor = list(yes = c("copper wire", "a steel nail", "an aluminium can", "salt water",
                           "graphite", "a silver spoon"),
                   no = c("a rubber band", "dry wood", "a glass rod", "a plastic ruler", "air",
                          "pure water"), b = 0.5),
  renewable = list(yes = c("wind", "sunlight", "tides", "geothermal heat", "moving water", "biomass"),
                   no = c("coal", "oil", "natural gas", "uranium", "peat", "diesel"), b = -0.4),
  physical = list(yes = c("ice melting", "sugar dissolving in water", "glass breaking",
                          "water boiling", "wax melting", "salt crystals forming as water evaporates"),
                  no = c("wood burning", "iron rusting", "milk souring", "bread baking",
                         "a match burning", "baking soda fizzing in vinegar"), b = 0.9))
label <- c(mammal = "a mammal", reptile = "a reptile", insect = "an insect", metal = "a metal",
           conductor = "a good conductor of electricity", renewable = "a renewable energy source",
           physical = "an example of a physical change")
contexts <- c("A class is sorting cards for a science display.",
              "Ms Okafor gives her students a quick review question.",
              "Students are making a poster for the school science fair.")
rows <- list()
for (g in names(groups)) for (i in 1:10) {
  neg <- i > 5
  gr <- groups[[g]]
  key <- sample(if (neg) gr$no else gr$yes, 1)
  opts <- sample(c(key, sample(if (neg) gr$yes else gr$no, 3)))
  stem <- sprintf("Which of these is %s%s?", if (neg) "NOT " else "", label[[g]])
  if (i %% 2 == 0) stem <- paste(sample(contexts, 1), stem)
  rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    id = sprintf("S%s%02d", toupper(substr(g, 1, 3)), i), topic = g, stem = stem,
    A = opts[1], B = opts[2], C = opts[3], D = opts[4], key = LETTERS[match(key, opts)])
}
sci <- do.call(rbind, rows)
f <- item_features(sci)
b_true <- sapply(sci$topic, function(g) groups[[g]]$b) + 0.7 * f$negation +
  0.25 * (f$sentences - 1) - 0.3 * f$key_longest + rnorm(nrow(sci), 0, 0.25)
theta <- rnorm(1000)
resp <- sapply(b_true, function(b) rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(theta - b)))
colnames(resp) <- sci$id
rasch <- mirt(as.data.frame(resp), 1, "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
sci$b <- -coef(rasch, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]   # Rasch difficulty
```

`item_features()` reads the stem and the options and returns one row of
features per item: Length, sentences, readability (`grade`), numbers,
negation, the length of the options, whether the key is the longest option,
and each item's most similar other item.

```{r}
feats <- item_features(sci)
feats[c(1, 2, 6), c("id", "words", "sentences", "grade", "negation", "key_longest")]
items <- merge(sci, feats)
round(cor(items[, c("words", "sentences", "grade", "negation", "key_longest")], items$b), 2)
```

Negated items are harder, and so are longer ones; a longest key goes with
easier items. Now predict difficulty from four text features with three
models. `predict_difficulty()` fits each model five times, each time
predicting the fifth of the items it did not see:

```{r}
text <- c("sentences", "negation", "option_words", "key_longest")
m1 <- predict_difficulty(items, text)
m1
```

On items they have not seen, the two linear models explain a little under
60% of the variance in difficulty ($R^2$), with a typical error (RMSE) of
about 0.4 logits. The random forest does worse: With 70 items and effects
that simply add up, its flexibility buys nothing. The LLTM's weights say
what the features do:

```{r}
tidy(m1)[tidy(m1)$method == "lltm", ]
```

A negation adds about two thirds of a logit, a context sentence about 0.2,
and a longest key makes an item easier, as item writers would expect.
`option_words` has a large weight too, which is less plausible as a cause:
Long options belong to the harder topics, such as physical changes. The
features know nothing about topic, so they stand in for it where they can.
Adding the topic as a feature brings the error down to about 0.29 logits
(Exercise 1), close to the 0.25 of item-specific variation built into the
simulation, and the weight of `option_words` shrinks to almost nothing.

## Example 2: The one-step LLTM in mirt

The two-step LLTM treats the estimated difficulties as known. The one-step
LLTM fits the features to the responses directly: Each item's difficulty is
constrained to the weighted sum of its features. In mirt, the features are
passed as `itemdesign` and the model for them as `item.formula`. Here each
topic gets its own intercept:

```{r}
design <- data.frame(topic = factor(sci$topic), feats[, c("sentences", "negation", "key_longest")])
lltm <- mirt(as.data.frame(resp), 1, "Rasch", itemdesign = design,
             item.formula = ~ 0 + topic + sentences + negation + key_longest, verbose = FALSE)
v <- mod2values(lltm)
eta <- v[v$item == sci$id[1] & v$name %in% c("sentences", "negation", "key_longest"),
         c("name", "value")]
eta$difficulty <- -eta$value   # mirt models easiness; reverse the sign for difficulty
eta
```

A context sentence adds about 0.2 logits, a negation about 0.6, and a
longest key makes an item about 0.3 logits easier: Close to the two-step
weights and to the values used to simulate the data. The classic test of
an LLTM compares it with the Rasch model, which gives every item its own
difficulty:

```{r}
anova(lltm, rasch)
```

Ten parameters cannot replace 70 free difficulties, and the likelihood
ratio test says so loudly; with 1,000 test takers it nearly always does.
The LLTM is still useful: It shows which features matter and by how much.
Explanatory IRT models that add a random item effect, so that each item may
differ from its features' prediction, combine the two views
[@deboeck2004]. They are generalized linear mixed models, and the eirm
package [@bulut2021] fits them with lme4 from data in long format, one row
per person and item. The model below keeps the LLTM's features and adds a
random effect for items, whose variance is the difficulty the features
leave unexplained (eirm reports easiness, so the signs are reversed again):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("eirm")
library(eirm)
long <- data.frame(person = rep(seq_len(nrow(resp)), ncol(resp)),
                   item = rep(colnames(resp), each = nrow(resp)),
                   resp = as.vector(resp))
long <- merge(long, data.frame(item = sci$id, design))
m_eirm <- eirm("resp ~ -1 + topic + sentences + negation + key_longest + (1|person) + (1|item)",
               data = long)
print(m_eirm, difficulty = TRUE)   # fixed effects as difficulties
lme4::VarCorr(m_eirm$model)       # person and residual item variance
```

The same framework adds person covariates, such as language status, and
their interactions with item features, which is DIF explained by features
rather than item by item.

## Example 3: New items or new kinds of items?

So far each fold held out random items, so every topic was in training. A
new item on a known topic is one question; a topic the model has never seen
is another. Hold out whole topics with `group`:

```{r}
m3 <- predict_difficulty(items, c("topic", "sentences", "negation", "key_longest"),
                         group = "topic", methods = "lltm")
m3$accuracy
```

With its topic held out, an item is predicted as if it belonged to an
average topic, and the error doubles to about 0.6 logits; $R^2$ falls to
about 0.15. The features still capture negation, the context sentence and
the longest key, but the topic, the largest part of an item's difficulty,
cannot be read off the text. This is the usual finding: Text features place
items within a family much better than they predict how hard a new kind of
item will be. That is why automatic item generation calibrates item models
rather than single items. Figure \@ref(fig:item-text-cv) shows the
predictions of Example 1, with random folds.

```{r item-text-cv, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Cross-validated predicted against estimated difficulty for the three models of Example 1. Points on the dashed line are predicted exactly; labels mark the worst-predicted items."}
autoplot(m1)
```

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Add `topic` to the features of Example 1, with random folds. How much
   does the error drop, and how do the LLTM weights of `negation`,
   `key_longest` and `option_words` change?
2. A colleague adds `p_pilot`, the proportion correct in this year's field
   test, to the features. Compute it from `resp`, add it to `items`, and
   run `predict_difficulty()`. What does the output warn you about, and
   why is the model useless for new items?
3. Without `topic`, the two-step LLTM with `sentences`, `negation` and
   `key_longest` gives `key_longest` a weight near zero. Why? Look at
   `table(items$key_longest, items$topic)`.
4. Look at the `similarity` and `nearest` columns of `feats`. Which items
   are most alike, and are any of them near-duplicates?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. topic as a feature
m_topic <- predict_difficulty(items, c("topic", text))
m_topic$accuracy
w <- tidy(m_topic)
w[w$method == "lltm" & !grepl("topic", w$term), ]

# 2. a leaky feature
items$p_pilot <- colMeans(resp)[items$id]
predict_difficulty(items, c(text, "p_pilot"), methods = "lltm")

# 3. key_longest without topic
tidy(predict_difficulty(items, c("sentences", "negation", "key_longest"), methods = "lltm"))
table(items$key_longest, items$topic)

# 4. the most similar items
head(feats[order(-feats$similarity), c("id", "nearest", "similarity")])
```

1. The RMSE drops from about 0.42 to 0.29 and $R^2$ rises to about 0.8 for
   the linear models; the forest stays behind (about 0.41). `negation`
   (about 0.63) and `key_longest` (about -0.34) are close to the simulated
   0.7 and -0.3, while `option_words` falls from about 0.5 to 0.1 with a
   large standard error: It was standing in for the topic.
2. The model predicts almost perfectly, and the printout flags `p_pilot`:
   Its rank correlation with $b$ is -1. The proportion correct and the
   Rasch difficulty are computed from the same responses, so the feature
   *is* the label in disguise. A new item has no field-test data, so the
   model cannot be used for it.
3. Five of the 16 items with a longest key are on physical changes, the
   hardest topic, whose options are long. Without the topic in the model,
   the easiness that a longest key brings is cancelled by the difficulty of
   the topic it comes with. An LLTM weight is only as good as the features
   left out of the model, as in any regression.
4. The most alike pairs (similarity about 0.75) are items on the same topic
   with the same stem and context sentence and one or two shared options.
   They are different items written from one template. A similarity close
   to 1, with the same options, would mark a near-duplicate that should not
   appear on the same form.

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Fischer [-@fischer1973] introduced the LLTM, and De Boeck and Wilson
[-@deboeck2004] place it in the family of explanatory item response models.
AlKhuzaey et al. [-@alkhuzaey2024] and Benedetto et al. [-@benedetto2023]
review difficulty prediction from text, from the education and the
computer science sides. Yaneva et al. [-@yaneva2024] report a shared task
on real licensing-exam items, a useful reality check. Bulut, Gorgun and
Yildirim-Erbasli [-@bulut2021] show how to fit explanatory extensions of
dichotomous and polytomous Rasch models in R with eirm.
